idea.body: Every triangle's three angles always add up to 180 degrees, no matter its shape or size. A ramp's support brace forms a triangle with a base angle of 50 degrees and a second angle of 70 degrees. The third angle is 180 minus 50 minus 70, which is 60 degrees. A triangle with all three angles under 90 degrees is acute. One with a 90 degree angle is right, and one with an angle over 90 degrees is obtuse. A triangle can also be named by its sides. Three equal sides make it equilateral, two equal sides make it isosceles, and no equal sides make it scalene.

figure.alt: A ramp support triangle with angles 50 degrees, 70 degrees, and an unknown angle.

workedExample.prompt: A kite's frame is a triangle with one angle of 90 degrees and another of 35 degrees. Find the third angle, then say whether the triangle is a right triangle.
steps: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees.
Add the two known angles: 90 + 35 = 125 degrees.
Subtract from 180 to find the third: 180 - 125 = 55 degrees.
Since one angle is exactly 90 degrees, the kite's frame is a right triangle.

figure.alt: A kite frame drawn as a right triangle with angles 90 degrees, 35 degrees, and an unknown angle.

ways.name: The angle sum is 180
ways.when: Use this any time you know two of a triangle's three angles.
steps: A frame is a triangle with one angle of 90 degrees and another of 35 degrees.
The three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees.
Add the two known angles: 90 plus 35 is 125 degrees.
Subtract from 180 to find the third: 180 minus 125 is 55.
Since one angle is exactly 90 degrees, the triangle is a right triangle.
ways.example: A frame is a triangle with angles 90 degrees and 35 degrees. Find the third angle.
ways.trap: Subtracting only one known angle from 180 and forgetting the second one.

figure.alt: A kite frame drawn as a right triangle with angles 90 degrees, 35 degrees, and an unknown third angle.

ways.name: The exterior angle rule
ways.when: Use this when one side of the triangle is extended and you want the outside angle it makes.
steps: A triangle has interior angles of 50 degrees and 60 degrees at two of its corners.
One side is extended past the third corner, making an exterior angle there.
The exterior angle always equals the sum of the two angles not next to it.
Add the two remote angles: 50 plus 60 is 110.
ways.example: A triangle has interior angles 50 degrees and 60 degrees. Find the exterior angle at the third corner.
ways.trap: Adding the exterior angle's own neighbouring interior angle instead of the two remote ones.

figure.alt: A triangle with one side extended past a vertex, showing the two known interior angles, 50 degrees and 60 degrees, and the unknown exterior angle.

frames.caption: Extend a side: exterior angle formed.
Exterior equals the two remote angles.

ways.name: Isosceles base angles are equal
ways.when: Use this when two sides of the triangle are equal and the apex angle is known.
steps: An isosceles triangle has an apex angle of 40 degrees.
Its two base angles are equal to each other, so call each one x.
The three angles add to 180: 40 plus x plus x equals 180.
2x equals 140, so x equals 70.
ways.example: An isosceles triangle has an apex angle of 40 degrees. Find each base angle.
ways.trap: Splitting 180 into three equal parts instead of accounting for the apex angle first.

figure.alt: An isosceles triangle with an apex angle of 40 degrees and two equal base angles, each labelled x.

frames.caption: Base angles are equal: each x.

ways.name: Right triangle shortcut
ways.when: Use this when you already know the triangle has a right angle in it.
steps: A right triangle has one angle of 90 degrees and another of 24 degrees.
The two non-right angles of a right triangle always add up to 90 degrees.
Subtract the known angle from 90 instead of from 180: 90 minus 24 is 66.
ways.example: A right triangle has one angle of 90 degrees and another of 24 degrees. Find the third.
ways.trap: Subtracting from 180 out of habit instead of using the faster 90 degree shortcut.
